content.overview: BNS s. 48 — Abetment outside India for offence in India.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
New. Abetment outside India of an offence committed in India is now expressly covered — closing a territorial gap the IPC left open. A BNS provision with no single IPC predecessor. Treat it as a fresh offence.
In student language: BNS s. 48 is the rule on “Abetment outside India for offence in India”. The section provides that a person abets an offence within the meaning of this Sanhita who, without and beyond India, abets the commission of any act in India which would constitute an offence if committed in India. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 48 exists so that “Abetment outside India for offence in India” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
48. A person abets an offence within the meaning of this Sanhita who, without and beyond India, abets the commission of any act in India which would constitute an offence if committed in India

Essential ingredients
1. A person abets an offence within the meaning of this Sanhita who, without and beyond India, abets the commission of any act in India which would constitute an offence if committed in India

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A, in country X, instigates B, to commit a murder in India, A is guilty of abetting murder

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 48 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

learningObjectives: Understand the extraterritorial reach of BNS s. 48 covering foreign abettors targeting India.
Analyze the territorial nexus created when the target offence or consequence occurs in India.
Identify procedural requirements for trying foreign abettors.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 48 provides that a person who, outside India, abets the commission of any offence in India is liable to be dealt with, tried and punished as if the abetment had been committed within India.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Sovereign penal jurisdiction extends to foreign actors who initiate or support criminal acts aimed at the territory, security, or citizens of India, ensuring that international boundaries cannot be exploited to escape liability.
statutoryFramework: Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt, BNS s. 48.
Geographic nexus: The abettor acts 'outside India'.
Target location: The offence is intended to be committed or is committed 'in India'.
Legal fiction: Dealt with, tried, and punished 'as if the abetment had been committed within India'.
essentialIngredients: The abetting acts (planning, financing, cyber-direction, arms supply) occurred outside India.
The object of the abetment was an offence committed or attempted in India.
The person is subject to Indian jurisdiction upon extradition or presence in India.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 48 is the mirror provision to Section 47. It addresses modern cross-border challenges such as foreign terrorist handlers, transnational cybercrime syndicates, and overseas drug cartels. An operative sitting in another country who transmits instructions, funds, or cyber-malware to perpetrators within India to carry out riots, assassinations, or financial fraud is deemed to have committed abetment within India. Once apprehended or extradited, he faces trial under Indian law.
examples: Teaching example (Foreign cyber-handler): An overseas hacker sitting in country X provides stolen credentials and malicious scripts to an accomplice in Bengaluru to breach an Indian banking server. Section 48 confers jurisdiction on Indian courts to try the overseas hacker.

Teaching example (Overseas arms supplier): An arms dealer in country Y ships hidden firearms into Mumbai to support a planned gang war. The dealer is liable under s. 48 as an abettor of the offences committed in Mumbai.
distinctions: Section 47 vs Section 48: Section 47 covers acts in India targeting foreign territory; Section 48 covers acts abroad targeting Indian territory.
Extradition requirements: Section 48 provides the substantive penal basis, while extradition treaties and BNSS regulate the procedural arrest.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a foreign national operating a digital fraud server outside India who instructed agents in Delhi to withdraw defrauded cash can be prosecuted under BNS.
Rule: BNS s. 48 makes any person outside India who abets an offence in India liable as if the abetment occurred in India.
Application: The target offence of cheating and theft was executed in Delhi. The foreign handler's abetment falls directly under s. 48.
Conclusion: Indian courts have jurisdiction to try the handler.

Cite cross-border terrorism or cyber-fraud as practical examples.
